article.overview: A thermal insulation experiment tests how insulating materials and assemblies, such as multilayer insulation (MLI) blankets, thermal shrouds and insulating coatings, keep lunar equipment, structures or cryogenic fluids within a workable temperature range. The catalogue entry is generic, so this article describes the experiment class rather than one defined mission. The directly relevant evidence is mostly ground testing and vendor or engineering reports. The flown lunar examples are an Apollo-era thermal blanket that was lost during an ascent, and in-situ measurements of regolith thermal properties by Chandrayaan-3 and by the LISTER probe on Blue Ghost Mission 1. No published flight dataset was found for a dedicated lunar insulation-performance experiment.
article.description: An insulation experiment measures how well a material or system limits heat flow between the warm and cold parts of a system, and how that performance changes in the lunar environment. On the Moon the surface is exposed to vacuum, large day and night temperature changes, radiation, micrometeoroid impacts and dust. A test may use a flight or flight-like insulation article on a lander or surface platform, or a ground-based test article whose results are compared with models. Typical measured quantities include temperatures on the warm and cold sides of the insulation, heat flux, the temperature profile through the layers and, for cryogenic storage, evaporation rate or boil-off. The catalogue does not specify which of these a payload would measure, so this description is a general engineering framework rather than the specification of one payload.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose is primarily engineering rather than geophysical. An insulation experiment can verify that a design performs as predicted in vacuum and across lunar temperature cycles, support habitat and lander thermal design, and provide data for cryogenic propellant storage. A 2011 NASA Kennedy Space Center paper describes MLI testing for a methane tank sized like the Altair ascent tanks, and states that MLI performance depends on layer density, the number of layers and the warm boundary temperature [1]. Insulation test data also support thermal models of instruments and surface hardware. Measurements of the regolith itself, such as its thermal conductivity, are related but distinct, because the regolith is part of the thermal environment that insulation must work against (see Examples 4 and 5 under Physical Specifications and Engineering Characteristics).
article.operating_principle: Multilayer insulation reduces heat transfer mainly by radiation. It stacks many thin, reflective foil layers separated by low-conductivity spacers or netting. In vacuum, the gas that would otherwise carry heat by conduction is largely absent, so most of the remaining heat moves by radiation between layers and by conduction through the spacers and layer edges. Performance therefore depends on the number of layers, layer density, the quality of the reflective surfaces, the spacer design and the temperature of the warm boundary, which are the factors identified in NASA test work [1]. Insulation experiments usually combine sensors on the layers or surrounding structure with a time reference and a comparison against predictions. For regolith measurements the principle differs: a heated or thermal probe is inserted into the ground, and the regolith's conductivity is estimated from how the probe's temperature changes over time [6][8].
article.scientific_importance: Insulation is a design driver for almost every lunar system. The Apollo surface experiments show that passive thermal control was essential to surface hardware. The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package used insulation, reflectors and coatings, together with heaters and power-dissipating resistors, to control instrument temperatures [10]. Regolith thermal properties are also important, because they control how heat moves into and out of the ground, which affects heat-flow measurements and thermal models. Measurements from Chandrayaan-3 and the LISTER probe have begun to provide in-situ values for these properties [6][8]. Better insulation data would therefore support longer surface operations, more efficient cryogenic storage and more accurate thermal models of landers and habitats. Much of the present evidence comes from ground testing, which is valuable but cannot reproduce every lunar condition.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a thermal insulation experiment. Insulation is often a component of a larger lander, habitat or instrument rather than a stand-alone payload, and regolith probes are measurement devices rather than insulators. The examples below cover flown hardware, a flight-heritage claim reported by a vendor, ground tests, a flown regolith measurement, a flown subsurface probe and research-stage concepts. Only values stated in the cited sources are given, and where a figure is not publicly specified this is stated. Because the categories differ, the examples should not be compared directly.

examples.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Module descent-stage thermal blanket
examples.type: Flown lunar-surface insulation hardware (lost during ascent)
examples.status: Flown on Apollo 15; not an experiment in its own right.
examples.description: The Apollo 15 descent-stage thermal blanket is the best-documented flown example of lunar surface insulation hardware in the sources reviewed. NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal reports that it was lifted from near the Lunar Module's MESA by the ascent engine exhaust about 1.3 seconds after ascent-stage motion began. It flew about 110 m at an average ground speed of 20 m/s and struck the surface about 11 m north of the ALSEP Central Station, coming to rest about 70 m beyond it. NASA notes that a direct hit would likely have knocked the antenna out of alignment and lost data [2]. The page gives a flight time of about 5.5 to 5.6 seconds and an impact time of 6.9 seconds in the text and 6.8 seconds in a figure caption, so these timings should be quoted as approximate. The page does not describe the blanket's layer count or materials.
details: Mass, dimensions and layer count: not stated on the NASA page.
Materials: a secondary summary describes Mylar or Kapton multilayer blankets. This was not verified against primary Apollo documentation in this research.

examples.name: Quest Thermal integrated multilayer insulation (IMLI) on Robotic Refueling Mission 3
examples.type: Commercial MLI product; flight claimed by the vendor, Earth orbit only
examples.status: Vendor-reported flight heritage; not independently confirmed.
examples.description: Quest Thermal Group reports that its integrated multilayer insulation (IMLI), which uses discrete micro spacers rather than netting between layers, flew on the International Space Station payload Robotic Refueling Mission 3 (RRM3). The vendor states that the IMLI insulated the receiver tank after a launch on 5 December 2018 and describes this as TRL 9 through spaceflight [4]. These are vendor claims. The NASA RRM3 overview reviewed here describes the mission's purpose as on-orbit demonstration of cryogenic fuel storage and transfer. However, the abstract it provides does not mention IMLI, does not report results and does not confirm that the demonstration was completed [3]. The vendor also lists later flights, including a 2019 Green Propellant Infusion Mission, which were not independently verified. IMLI is therefore an Earth-orbit demonstration, not a lunar deployment.
details: Mass, dimensions and performance figures: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
A tank temperature below 82 K attributed to the IMLI in a secondary summary could not be confirmed in the NASA overview and is excluded.

examples.name: NASA methane tank MLI coupon and tank thermal tests (ground)
examples.type: Ground-based MLI test for a lunar surface methane tank
examples.description: NASA Kennedy Space Center work for the Methane Lunar Surface Thermal Control (MLSTC) effort tested MLI in a ground environment. A 2011 Cryogenic Engineering Conference paper by Johnson and Fesmire describes thermal performance testing of MLI coupons made the same way as the insulation on a tank about the size of the Altair ascent tanks. The coupons were tested in Cryostat-100 at the Cryogenics Test Laboratory [1]. The excerpt states that insulation performance depends on layer density, the number of layers and the warm boundary temperature, and that the tank testing simulates low Earth orbit and lunar surface conditions. The excerpt does not state the test duration, vacuum level, temperature range or measured heat leak. The title refers to liquid nitrogen, so the test fluid should be confirmed from the full paper before use.
details: Numerical performance (heat leak, boil-off, temperature range, test duration): not stated in the reviewed text.

examples.name: ChaSTE regolith thermal conductivity probe (Chandrayaan-3, Vikram lander)
examples.type: In-situ regolith thermal-property measurement (not an insulator)
examples.status: Flown on the Vikram lander; values taken from the indexed abstract.
examples.description: The ChaSTE thermal probe on the Vikram lander measured in-situ thermal conductivity of lunar regolith at a southern high-latitude site. A March 2025 Scientific Reports paper by Mathew et al. reports two active heating experiments at 80 mm depth giving 0.0115 ± 0.0008 and 0.0124 ± 0.0009 W m−1 K−1, and an inferred packing density of about 1940 ± 10 kg m−3 [6]. The probe carries ten temperature sensors and a heater near its tip and was driven into the regolith over about 29 hours [6]. An ISRO Space Physics Laboratory project page cites regolith conductivity below 0.03 W m−1 K−1 as a key challenge for in-situ probing, which is consistent with these values [7]. These values come from the abstract as indexed by search; the full text was not retrievable in this research and should be checked against the paper before use.
details: Probe power budget and mass: not stated in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: LISTER subsurface thermal probe (Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1)
examples.type: Flown subsurface thermal probe (regolith temperature and conductivity)
examples.status: Flown on Blue Ghost Mission 1 (CLPS TO-19D); preliminary heat-flow analysis only.
examples.description: The LISTER instrument (Lunar Instrumentation for Subsurface Thermal Exploration with Rapidity) flew on Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 1 (CLPS TO-19D) and was deployed in Mare Crisium in March 2025. NASA's Planetary Data System page describes it as the first robotically deployed subsurface thermal probe. It reached a depth of 1 m and measured temperature and thermal conductivity at eight depths [8]. The PDS page does not state a maximum design depth or the number of temperature sensors, and it reports that LISTER data were released on 9 January 2026 [8]. A 2026 EGU conference abstract indexed in search reports preliminary modelling suggesting a heat flow of about 13 to 14 mW m−2, compared with 16 mW m−2 for Apollo 17, but states that a fuller inversion was still in progress [9]. The heat-flow figure is preliminary and should not be treated as a final value.
details: Mass and power: not stated in the reviewed sources.

examples.name: Research-stage regolith-based and coated-Mylar insulation concepts
examples.description: Two research-stage developments show how insulation for lunar conditions may change. A University of Liege study describes a passive thermal shield made from an aerogel that combines lunar regolith, MXene and polyimide. The summary reviewed reports that regolith and MXene improve heat retention, but no quantitative values were verified in this research [11]. A University of Pennsylvania study, reported in a news article, describes flexible insulation made from coated Mylar. The article reports that coated stacks kept their insulating performance after 10 compression cycles, while uncoated stacks lost more, and that performance across the full lunar temperature range is still unknown [12]. The news report is a single secondary source, and the underlying paper was not located.
details: Mass, dimensions and power: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions apply to thermal insulation experiments. Insulation dimensions depend on the area to be protected and on the number of layers. The dimensions of the Apollo blanket are not stated on the NASA page, and the dimensions of the Quest IMLI and the NASA coupon and tank test articles were not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass and weight are not publicly specified for any example reviewed. For a future experiment, mass would drive launch and lander allocation, so it should be set from the intended test article rather than from these examples.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Passive insulation needs no power by itself. Active probes such as ChaSTE and LISTER need heating and data power, but their power budgets were not stated in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar insulation experiment must tolerate vacuum, large surface temperature swings, solar and radiative loads, micrometeoroid and dust exposure, and the exhaust and debris of nearby landing or ascent events. The Apollo 15 blanket example illustrates the last of these: ascent exhaust lifted a large insulation blanket about 110 m and created a hazard for nearby experiments [2]. Experiments that contact the regolith also need stable mounting, because probes depend on undisturbed ground. LISTER reached 1 m depth in this way [8]. Ground tests must represent the thermal boundary and vacuum conditions that the flight article will see [1]. The sources reviewed do not provide a verified lunar temperature range for a specific insulation test, so none is given here.
article.limitations: Ground coupon tests may not reproduce full-scale geometry, regolith contact or the complete lunar temperature cycle [1]. Insulation performance can decline when layers are compressed. This effect has been reported in a single news-level account [12]. Vendor performance claims were not independently confirmed [4]. Passive insulation is only as good as its installation and its interfaces with structures, and these interfaces are not specified in the sources reviewed. Regolith measurements are single-site or limited-depth results and cannot be generalised across the Moon. The catalogue entry does not define a specific payload, so this article covers the class of experiment. The LEMS lunar lander concept, which relies on heaters to survive the lunar night, was identified in a TFAWS 2020 abstract [5]. Its full text could not be read, so no figures from it are given.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A thermal insulation experiment could be carried as an element of a lander, a surface experiment package or a habitat test article. The transportation discussion therefore treats it as a surface payload, with notes for an integrated insulation article. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted, because no verified interface data were found for a specific insulation experiment.
transportation_process: Integrate the insulation article or test coupon into a lander or surface payload on Earth, including its mounting, thermal interfaces and any protective covers.
Launch the lander on a launch vehicle.
Transfer the spacecraft to the Moon.
Land the lander and protect the insulation from ascent or landing exhaust where the design requires it.
Deploy the experiment by exposing test articles to the surface or attaching the insulation to the hardware it protects.
Connect any heaters, sensors or data links and verify the thermal and data interfaces during commissioning.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment depends on the design. The Apollo 15 blanket was part of the Lunar Module and was not deployed as an experiment [2]. LISTER was deployed as a drilled subsurface probe on Blue Ghost Mission 1 [8], and ChaSTE was driven into the regolith by a motor-driven penetrator [6]. An insulation test article would normally be attached to the protected hardware or exposed as a coupon, with the method set by the lander design.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Historical examples are the Apollo 15 descent-stage blanket on a crewed lander [2], the vendor-reported Quest IMLI on RRM3, which flew to the ISS [3][4], and the LISTER and ChaSTE regolith measurements on Blue Ghost Mission 1 and Chandrayaan-3 [6][8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. NASA documents LISTER's presence on Blue Ghost Mission 1 [8], but that does not show that any insulation experiment is compatible with that lander.

article.historical_significance: Apollo-era thermal blankets and the passive thermal control of the Apollo surface experiments were among the first demonstrations of lunar surface thermal engineering in practice [2][10]. Since then the main developments have been cryogenic MLI testing for future lunar propulsion [1], an Earth-orbit demonstration of IMLI on the ISS that is vendor-reported [3][4], and in-situ regolith thermal measurements on Chandrayaan-3 and Blue Ghost Mission 1 [6][8]. No dedicated lunar insulation-performance experiment with published flight data was identified.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The catalogue does not define a specific payload for this entry, so the article covers a class of experiment. Key uncertainties include: no dedicated lunar insulation-performance experiment was identified; ChaSTE values come from an indexed abstract and have not been checked against the full text [6]; LISTER heat flow is preliminary [9]; IMLI flight performance is vendor-reported and was not confirmed by the NASA overview [3][4]; the Apollo blanket's layer count and materials rest on secondary sources; the statement on Apollo ALSEP passive thermal control relies on an archived encyclopedia article [10]; the LEMS concept's figures could not be retrieved [5]; the coated-Mylar results rest on one news report [12]; and no verified direct image assets were obtained. The research used seven web searches and nine page-read attempts, of which four pages were read in full, so the coverage is not exhaustive.

data_quality_notes: The catalogue entry is generic; the article covers the class of thermal insulation experiment rather than one defined mission.
No dedicated lunar insulation-performance experiment with published flight data was identified.
No direct image asset URLs were verified from official pages; the NASA pages read did not expose verified direct asset URLs, so no images are included.
ChaSTE values come from the indexed abstract. The publisher page redirected to a sign-in page and the DOAJ record returned HTTP 403, so the full text was not checked.
Sources disagree on the ChaSTE peak surface temperature (82 C in one source, 70 C in another); no temperature is used from them.
The Quest Thermal success-story PDF and the LEMS TFAWS abstract could not be parsed by WebFetch and no figures are taken from them. The LEMS abstract is cited only for the concept.
A 180-day surface storage requirement mentioned in a search summary was not confirmed in the fetched NASA report text and is excluded.
A tank temperature below 82 K attributed to IMLI in a search summary was not found in the NASA RRM3 overview and is excluded.
The Apollo 15 NASA page gives 5.5 and 5.6 s flight times and 6.9 and 6.8 s impact times in different places; both are noted as approximate.
The Liege and UPenn sources are abstract-level or news-level only.
The ALSEP passive thermal control statement relies on an archived encyclopedia article.
The LISTER heat-flow figure is preliminary and comes from a conference abstract indexed in search.
